In theory you can represent any finite set of actions as a prefix code, and then repeatedly generate both possible next bits (1 or 0), predict the value that an optimal action beginning with that bit would lead to, and choose the bit value that scores higher. This can be extended to countably infinite sets of actions, where each action can be described by a finite-length bit sequence. That doesn't get you all the way to continuity, but enables, for example, a single action to encode any finite number of numbers written out to any required level of precision, which should be enough for "engineering purposes".

It seems to me that the effectiveness of such a system would depend heavily on actions being encoded "well", so that at every bit position, the "meanings" of the subset of actions beneath that point in the tree are separated as well as possible by whether they begin with 1 or with 0.

It's a subtle question.

1) They may not be accounting for the size of the model, i.e. parameters, which is memorized by the system up front, which, if it scales exponentially with output length, would put a floor.

2) But then, does a model that memorizes require storage scaling exponentially with output length? Not always. When a model system gets large enough to memorize all the data, or especially when the model system is larger than the storage capacity of the brain, let's say, it stops requiring more storage to reproduce output losslessly.

3) There is still an innovation rate beyond memorization. Part of the new information being injected into language is entropy received from the universe, which is coming at a certain rate. Primitive example: let's say a model had 20% chance of making a mistake when performing a step, and 5% chance of immediately backtracking if it makes a mistake.

Now give this model a task that requires it to perform 25 steps to succeed. Success rate <1%.

Now, we RL this model, so that it has a 10% step mistake rate and a 50% mistake backtrack rate. Suddenly, the model performance jumps, and a significant amount of previously "impossible" successful rollouts appears.

This is how "small" changes can compound to a massive RL performance gain. The pieces were already present - the model was capable of both succeeding at a given step, and of backtracking if it didn't. But RL made them work together better.

In some cases, sharp application of SFT can accomplish the same results - with high sample efficiency and without paying the RL rollout tax. But that requires you to identify the "components of success" by hand, and then make a dataset targeting them. This doesn't scale like RL does.

Tokens into dimensions.

A good example is how humans talk about "left and right" in terms of political systems.

Humans are able to intuitively place these complicated multivariable economic-political systems into a one dimensional line that we call left or right wing.

Of course, this deep compression complicates things... why is national socialism considered right, while democratic socialism is considered left.

You can get more signal by increasing dimensions, so let's say instead just left or right, we have 2 axis one for economic and one for political. This would make things more clear. AI is doing this to text. It ingests text, and creates a token vocabulary. IIRC most models have a vocab of hundreds to low thousands of tokens.

This token vocabulary (how many distinct tokens it uses) is how many dimensions the AI thinks in, so to speak.

After this, there is the whole training process of how tokens relate to each other.

Isn't applicable, as it doesn't compress anything we would call a question or answer.

Instead, answers to questions are an emergent property of how text fragments relate to each other, and is why it can give contradictory answers.

And then those elements can be recombined into the near-infinite permutations to decompress. The compressor finds the commonalities and exploits them to fit "infinite" into "finite" better.

This is kind of hard to explain but I feel like there is a difference between a generalized representation and what I understand to be happening in an LLM. From what I gather, LLMs have a high dimensional space and there are thousands of vectors involved in predicting the next token, so for example if I ask it to download a youtube video, there may be shared activation spaces around downloading a video, which shifts the distributions of tokens towards tokens related to downloading a youtube video. But does it for example generalize the concept of downloading? Do all prompts related to any kind of downloading share vector spaces and are generalized? This seems wrong to me but I could be wrong.

Also is it really true that it can create compressed representations that decompose? Like I feel like to understand tools and specific scenarios you need agent skills and training data about the tool. It can't just learn from something else. So there _is_ a lot of specialized instances of data about all kinds of things. The higher level goal of "downloading a youtube video" doesn't really matter in the grand scheme of things, it only matters as much as it helps the LLM find the right text to produce. Like in my example it may be that if I used the keyword "yt-dlp" in the prompt that would matter a lot more than "download a video".

Why not?

If our objective is, for example, "compress the sum of all of humankind's knowledge", then we have a bit of a conundrum: that objective contains human knowledge of math, but also of religion, and of soap opera plots.

You, a human, could easily make an argument that one of those things is more important than the others, and thus should dominate. But an optimal compressor does not care. All of those things are in its objective. It weights them accordingly. It will compress both math and soap opera into its "universal information state" - and if it finds patterns that happen to help compress both, then all the better for it.

As such, if we take "compressor" as LLM and "objective" as its training datasets, a capable LLM would be able to both solve math problems and give a preacher-like sermon. But it would not let its knowledge of religion intrude into its performance in math, or the other way around, to an unwarranted level. The compressor lives by "non-overlapping magisteria."

> You can write a script in an endless amount of programming languages, you can segment the task into an almost innumerable set of sub steps (for example different scripts for different steps in the process), so what exactly does compression of that information mean when it can be compressed and predicted in so many different ways?

It means that, instead of storing every possible permutation, we get a compressed representation that decomposes - separates "segment a video" from "write code in language A" or "use tool B". And then those elements can be recombined into the near-infinite permutations to decompress. The compressor finds the commonalities and exploits them to fit "infinite" into "finite" better.

Saturation means that the pretraining data has inherent entropy, even if we can't properly evaluate it. Absolutely the improvements in perplexity on the held-out OpenAI codebase dataset are due to more relevant samples in the training corpus and general improvements in data quality.

We assume that there is some point where the base models will reach the limits of inherent entropy for codebase quality. That there are fundamentally irreducible factors and unknowns that dictate resource-constrained and information-constrained performance.

Perplexity on any holdout dataset has limits to its usefulness as a measure and goes back to the eval and standardisation question.

Why the "saturated" requirement?

One way to improve perplexity would be to obtain pre-training signal (raw data, or something like data generators, distillation teachers) that give the model a lasting perplexity edge - teaches it effective, general patterns.

Using perplexity as a standard measure makes sense when we assume that data for pretraining is essentially finite, or otherwise saturated. You would expect holdout datasets for perplexity to be similar across labs, given the distribution of pretraining data.

At this stage of model development, post-training RL hillclimbing may confound recent model developments in terms of evaluating their useful capabilities e.g. "Solved a Millenium Math problem". It would be useful to see how different checkpoints would solve an equivalent (or the same) problem i.e. post-train multiple checkpoints of a pretrained model at varying base model perplexity. Perplexity is not defined in the article. FYI:

Perplexity is the degree of surprise the model has in predicting the next token, over a sequence of tokens. At the worst case, perplexity is equal to the size of the vocabulary. At the best case, perplexity is 1.

So, given a sequence of tokens, "e = m c ^ 2", if the p(token | prev tokens) = 1 for every token, perplexity ends up being 1. If, however, it's a random predictor, the p(token | prev tokens) is 1/vocab for every token, and perplexity ends up being len(vocab).

The article plots log(perplexity) on the y-axis, which puts the best case at 0 (i.e. log 1).

The perplexity / intelligence correspondence is one of those ideas that is surprising at first, but in retrospect could not work any other way.
